beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about how old the evidence behind a financial report actually is. Today we are going to learn why that never shows up in the numbers, and what happened when I measured it on my own project. The answer was not flattering.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the subject
three output lines land, ending on 148 days

props.command: How old is the data behind this report, and does the report say so anywhere?
output: A report about February looks identical whether the data is a week old or a year old.
There are two separate gaps, and neither appears in any figure.
Measured on my own shipped pack, one of them is 148 days.

beats.narration_text: There are exactly two gaps and they are different problems. Arrival lag is the time between a period closing and the data about it being produced. Shelf age is the time between the data being produced and somebody reading it. A report can be perfectly fresh on one and badly stale on the other.

show.event: 'Neither is in the numbers' lands in terracotta

layers.title: Neither is in the numbers

props.caption: A report can be fine on one gap and disqualified by the other.

beats.narration_text: So I pointed it at my own verified pack, the one every report in this project has been built from. February closed on the twenty-eighth. The data describing it was created on the twenty-sixth of July. That is a hundred and forty-eight days of arrival lag, and the engine calls it stale.

show.event: period and close date write on
the two gaps appear, 148 and 92 days
the verdict STALE lands in terracotta

beats.narration_text: Now, measuring is the easy half. The harder question is what the engine should do when it cannot measure at all, and there are two cases where reporting a number would be worse than refusing to.

props.title: When Measuring Is the Wrong Answer
props.body: Two cases where producing a freshness number would be worse than refusing to produce one.

beats.narration_text: The second one is this. If the data was created before the period it describes had even finished, that is not stale data. That is impossible data. A pack cannot report on a month that had not ended when the pack was made, so the engine refuses rather than returning a cheerful negative lag.

show.event: the comment writes on, naming the distinction
the comparison holds as the voice says 'impossible'

props.title: freshness.py — the impossibility check
props.code:
# The impossibility check. Data cannot describe a period that had not
# finished when the data was made. This is not staleness; it is a defect.
if created_on < ends:
    raise FreshnessError(
        f"provenance.created_on {created_on.isoformat()} precedes the end of "
        f"period {period} ({ends.isoformat()}); the pack cannot describe a "
        "period that had not finished"
    )

beats.narration_text: And that is what it says when you try it. A pack claiming February, created on the tenth of February. Eighteen days before the month ended. The engine names the dates and stops. Without that check it would have reported a lag of minus eighteen days and nobody reading a report would ever see it.

show.event: the first line of the refusal writes on
the period and its true end date land
the closing clause holds in terracotta

props.artifactTitle: a pack created before its own period closed
props.artifactHeading: The refusal, in the engine's own words
artifactLines: a period that had not finished

beats.narration_text: The first case is quieter and more common. A pack with no provenance file at all. The tempting default is to treat missing information as fine, because nothing looks wrong. But absence of evidence about age is not evidence of freshness, so that is refused too.

show.event: caption: none of these is treated as fresh

items: A date that cannot be parsed
A period the engine cannot read
props.caption: Each of these is refused. None of them is treated as fresh.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT IT WILL NOT TELL YOU
beats.narration_text: Here is the limit, and it is the whole reason this reports rather than blocks. A hundred and forty-eight days is routine for an annual audit and disqualifying for a weekly flash report. Same number, opposite verdicts, and nothing in the data says which one you are holding. So the limits are supplied, never derived.

the weekly flash row stacks on, same number
'The engine cannot tell' lands in terracotta

props.caption: So it measures and states. It does not decide.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT IT WILL NOT TELL YOU
beats.narration_text: Which gives three questions worth asking of any report somebody hands you. When did the period close. When was the data made. And when did you read it. If a report cannot answer all three, its freshness is unknown, and unknown is not the same as fine.

props.destTitle: is unknown until all three are answered
props.arcCaption: unknown is not the same as fine

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT IT WILL NOT TELL YOU
beats.narration_text: And I left my own pack stale rather than regenerating it to make the number look better. The hundred and forty-eight days is real. A freshness check whose first act is to hide its own first finding would not be worth shipping.

props.title: I Left the Number Where It Was
props.body: The 148 days is real. A freshness check whose first act is to hide its own first finding would not be worth shipping.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. A financial report carries two ages that never appear in any figure: how long the data took to arrive after the period closed, and how long it then sat before anyone read it. Measured on this project's own shipped pack, the arrival lag is a hundred and forty-eight days and the verdict is stale. A pack with no provenance is refused rather than assumed fresh, and a pack created before its own period ended is refused as impossible rather than reported as merely late. The limits are supplied, because the same lag is routine for one kind of report and disqualifying for another, and nothing in the data says which one you are holding.

props.artifactHeading: Two ages, neither of them in the numbers
artifactLines: Arrival lag and shelf age are separate gaps, and no figure in a report shows either.
On this project's own pack: 148 days of lag, 92 days of age, verdict STALE.
No provenance is refused, not assumed fresh. Absence of evidence about age proves nothing.
Data created before its period closed is refused as impossible, not reported as late.
Limits are supplied. The same lag is routine for an audit and fatal for a flash report.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a dashboard or report I rely on and tell me, for every number on it, when the underlying data was last refreshed and how you worked that out. Then tell me which numbers you could not date at all. Run that on something you actually check. The undateable ones are the interesting answer, because people trust those exactly as much as the rest.

props.command: Take a dashboard or report I rely on. For every number on it, tell me when the underlying data was last refreshed and how you worked that out. Then tell me which numbers you could not date at all.
output: The undateable numbers are the answer. People trust those exactly as much as the rest.
If a figure cannot be dated, its freshness is unknown, not fine.

beats.narration_text: That was evidence freshness for the Mycroft Finance Investigator. The code and the tests are in pull request seventeen. Adwait Changan, for Humanitarians AI.
